quotes.text: It's often cited as one of the first albums to feature what would later become signature phrases and techniques associated with the electro genre, as well as a benchmark recording in synth-pop – and to lesser extent – a precursor to hip hop – the latter being in regard to the album's 9th track – 'Was Dog A Doughnut'.
his early 70s output consistently delivered music of the highest quality that would consequently influence singer-songwriters and guitar-based pop for generations.

Stevens overcame his illness and reinvented himself – reemerging a completely different artist with a new-found zeal – surprising many by returning to the music industry an almost unrecognizable figure.

After basking in success for several years at the start of the decade, Cat's standards began to decline – and with it – his popularity. After a couple of years of waning public interest during the mid-70s – and several attempts to branch out into other genres – Stevens was struggling to find direction and identity.
still in pursuit of something new to revivify his career trajectory – Cat released his milestone tenth studio album – the enigmatically titled 'Izitso'.
The album has four stone cold classics – plus a lot of songs that had some potential, but ones where the ever estimable Cat could have used someone to workshop his songs with.

However impressive and inspiring it is to think of an individual artist having a grand, individual, uncompromised, singular creative vision that is theirs and theirs alone, I think The Beatles are the perfect example of why it is far better to have a partner or small group of partners to take your songs out to the woodshed with and whip them into shape.

Teaser and the Firecat is a great album, but I can't help thinking how much greater and album it could have been had Cat had a Lennon-or-McCartney-like partner to give him some feedback and helpful suggestions.

There is something so natural, so primal about that opening guitar part and that gorgeous melody – it's like the song is as old as Creation and has been hanging around in the ether for the right artistic soul to discover it. It's like something that has been buried in the depths of our collective unconscious waiting through centuries of generations for a starry-eyed singer-songwriter to excavate it and set it free again on the world.
It's like Stevens reached out a hand and snatched an ancient, timeless, beloved melody out of a passing breeze and set it to song.
It's so clever the way he talks about how if he ever loses his eyes, his hands or his mouth, and he'll come back with the most glass-half-full response imaginable.
The more or less chronological order of the tracks nicely illustrates Cat's rapid improvement as a songwriter – and gradual decline.

The artist now known as Yusuf/Cat Stevens did more than borrow from his own catalog for his latest album. He also reunited with the producer and acoustic guitarist who worked on his seminal hits from the 1970s, resulting in a new album that sounds like old Cat Stevens with even more light and wisdom than before.
Fifty years after Cat Stevens' debut album, "The Laughing Apple" blends reimagined songs from 1967 with new compositions and newly completed 50-year-old unfinished tracks.

Yet with Alun Davies' sparkling guitars and Paul Samwell-Smith's crisp production, the 11 songs sound like a cohesive set of tunes that always belonged together, and carry through themes of so much of Yusuf/Cat Stevens' music: love and the joy of childhood.
